targets.name: Hydrophilic head
targets.description: The polar phosphate-containing head interacts with water outside the cell or in the cytosol.

targets.name: Hydrophobic tails
targets.description: The two nonpolar fatty-acid tails face the interior of the bilayer, away from water.

targets.name: Cholesterol
targets.description: Cholesterol sits among the lipid tails and helps regulate membrane fluidity and stability.

targets.name: Channel protein
targets.description: A membrane-spanning protein provides a selective, water-friendly passage through the hydrophobic bilayer.

targets.name: Glycoprotein
targets.description: A protein with an outward-facing carbohydrate chain. Such tags participate in recognition and other interactions.

targets.name: Glycocalyx
targets.description: Carbohydrate chains on proteins and lipids form an extracellular coat involved in protection, recognition, and adhesion.

targets.name: Glycolipid
targets.description: A lipid with an attached carbohydrate chain facing the extracellular fluid.

targets.name: Peripheral protein
targets.description: This protein associates with one membrane surface rather than crossing the entire bilayer.

targets.name: Plasma membrane
targets.description: The selectively permeable boundary separates the cytoplasm from extracellular fluid.

targets.name: Nucleus
targets.description: Houses most cellular DNA and is the site of transcription; its envelope separates it from the cytoplasm.

targets.name: Nucleolus
targets.description: Produces ribosomal RNA and assembles ribosomal subunits inside the nucleus.

targets.name: Rough endoplasmic reticulum
targets.description: Membrane sacs with attached ribosomes make proteins destined for secretion, membranes, or certain organelles.

targets.name: Smooth endoplasmic reticulum
targets.description: A ribosome-free membrane network involved in lipid synthesis, calcium storage, and detoxification.

targets.name: Golgi apparatus
targets.description: Stacked flattened sacs modify, sort, and package products arriving from the ER.

targets.name: Mitochondrion
targets.description: Its folded inner membrane supports much of the cell’s aerobic ATP production.

targets.name: Lysosome
targets.description: Contains digestive enzymes that break down worn-out components and material brought into the cell.

targets.name: Peroxisome
targets.description: Carries out oxidative reactions; catalase helps convert hydrogen peroxide to water and oxygen.

targets.name: Centrioles
targets.description: A paired set of cylindrical microtubule structures in the centrosome near the nucleus.

targets.name: Free ribosomes
targets.description: Unbound ribosomes translate mRNA into proteins, including many used in the cytosol.

targets.name: Transport vesicle
targets.description: A small membrane-bound carrier moves cargo between organelles or to the plasma membrane.

targets.name: Cytosol
targets.description: The fluid portion of the cytoplasm around organelles. Cytoplasm includes both cytosol and organelles outside the nucleus.

organelles-cytoskeleton.title: The cell’s support network
organelles-cytoskeleton.description: Three filament types, enlarged separately. The small lower sketches connect filament structure to cellular movement and anchoring.

targets.name: Microtubule
targets.description: A hollow tubulin cylinder; resists compression, forms intracellular transport tracks, and participates in the spindle, cilia, and flagella.

targets.name: Microfilament
targets.description: Thin intertwined actin chains; important for cell shape, muscle contraction, and the cleavage furrow during cytokinesis.

targets.name: Intermediate filament
targets.description: Rope-like protein fibers resist tension and help anchor cells and organelles.

targets.name: Cilia
targets.description: Numerous short microtubule-based projections move material along a cell surface, as in the airways.

targets.name: Flagellum
targets.description: The long microtubule-based projection that propels a sperm cell; sperm are the only flagellated human cells.

targets.name: Cytoskeletal anchoring
targets.description: Intermediate filaments attach to cellular junctions, helping tissues resist pulling forces.

targets.name: Nuclear envelope
targets.description: Two lipid bilayers enclose the nucleus; the outer membrane is continuous with the rough ER.

targets.name: Nuclear pore
targets.description: A regulated passage through the envelope. RNA and ribosomal subunits leave; many proteins enter.

targets.name: Nucleolus
targets.description: A region where rRNA is produced and ribosomal subunits are assembled; it has no enclosing membrane.

targets.name: Chromatin
targets.description: DNA plus associated proteins within the nucleus. It condenses into visible chromosomes during division.

targets.name: DNA double helix
targets.description: Two antiparallel strands with sugar-phosphate backbones and complementary bases: A pairs with T; C with G.

targets.name: Nucleosome
targets.description: A length of DNA wrapped around histone proteins, the basic repeating unit of chromatin packaging.

targets.name: Replicated chromosome
targets.description: A condensed chromosome after replication has two sister chromatids joined at a centromere. Each chromatid contains a DNA molecule.

targets.name: Homologous chromosome
targets.description: The corresponding chromosome inherited from the other parent. Homologs carry the same kinds of genes but can have different alleles.

targets.name: Parental DNA
targets.description: Before copying, the two complementary DNA strands are paired together.

targets.name: Helicase
targets.description: Unwinds and separates the paired DNA strands at the replication fork.

targets.name: Template strand
targets.description: Each original strand supplies the base sequence that directs synthesis of its new complementary strand.

targets.name: DNA polymerase
targets.description: Adds complementary nucleotides to the growing DNA strand. New DNA is synthesized in the 5′ to 3′ direction.

targets.name: New DNA strand
targets.description: The newly assembled strand is complementary to its template. DNA polymerase and other enzymes also help limit copying errors.

targets.name: Free nucleotides
targets.description: Building blocks available for incorporation into a new DNA strand.

targets.name: Semiconservative product
targets.description: Each completed daughter DNA molecule contains one pre-existing strand and one newly synthesized strand.

targets.name: Coding DNA strand
targets.description: Its sequence matches the RNA transcript except DNA uses T where RNA uses U. It is not the strand read as the template.

targets.name: Template DNA strand
targets.description: RNA polymerase reads this strand to build complementary RNA.

targets.name: RNA polymerase
targets.description: Opens a local transcription bubble and joins RNA nucleotides to extend the transcript.

targets.name: Growing pre-mRNA
targets.description: The initial RNA transcript is complementary to the DNA template strand. It is processed before translation.

targets.name: Exon
targets.description: A transcript segment retained in the mature RNA after splicing.

targets.name: Intron
targets.description: A transcript segment removed by the spliceosome during RNA processing.

targets.name: Mature mRNA
targets.description: Spliced RNA with joined exons; a 5′ cap and poly-A tail help protect it and support later translation.

targets.name: Poly-A tail
targets.description: A chain of adenine nucleotides added to the 3′ end of most eukaryotic mRNA.

protein-translation.title: Read the message, build the chain
protein-translation.description: The ribosome reads mRNA from 5′ to 3′. Complementary tRNA anticodons deliver amino acids in the encoded order.

targets.name: mRNA
targets.description: Carries the nucleotide message from DNA to a ribosome. The message is read in three-base codons.

targets.name: Ribosome
targets.description: Its large and small subunits position mRNA and tRNAs and catalyze peptide-bond formation.

targets.name: Codon
targets.description: A three-nucleotide unit in mRNA. For example, GAA specifies glutamate.

targets.name: tRNA
targets.description: An adapter RNA carries a specific amino acid and pairs its anticodon with a complementary mRNA codon.

targets.name: Anticodon
targets.description: A three-base sequence in tRNA; GGA pairs antiparallel with the illustrated CCU mRNA codon.

targets.name: Amino acid
targets.description: A building block of protein carried by a tRNA before being joined to the growing chain.

targets.name: Growing polypeptide
targets.description: Amino acids joined by peptide bonds; the completed chain will fold and may undergo further processing.

targets.name: Stop codon
targets.description: UAA, UAG, and UGA signal termination rather than specifying an amino acid.

division-cell-cycle.description: Move around the ring through growth, DNA synthesis, preparation, and division. The branch represents leaving the active division cycle. Durations are not to scale.

targets.name: G1 phase
targets.description: The cell grows, carries out normal functions, and produces cellular components before DNA synthesis.

targets.name: S phase
targets.description: DNA is replicated. Each chromosome acquires a sister chromatid; chromosome number does not double simply because DNA amount doubles.

targets.name: G2 phase
targets.description: Further growth, checks, and preparation for mitosis follow DNA replication.

targets.name: Mitotic phase
targets.description: Mitosis distributes duplicated chromosomes into two nuclei; cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.

targets.name: G0 phase
targets.description: A cell leaves the active division cycle. Some cells may re-enter; others remain outside the cycle while performing specialized functions.

targets.name: Sister chromatids
targets.description: Two copies of one replicated chromosome are joined at the centromere. A typical human cell has 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids after S phase.

targets.name: Cell-cycle checkpoints
targets.description: Regulatory checks help prevent progression when conditions or DNA integrity are unsuitable; cyclins and cyclin-dependent kinases regulate progression.

targets.name: Prophase
targets.description: Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes. The spindle forms; the nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down as division proceeds.

targets.name: Metaphase
targets.description: Duplicated chromosomes align individually along the cell equator, attached to spindle fibers from opposite poles.

targets.name: Anaphase
targets.description: Sister chromatids separate. Each is now a chromosome, moving toward an opposite pole.

targets.name: Telophase
targets.description: Chromosomes reach the poles; nuclear envelopes reform and chromosomes begin to decondense.

targets.name: Cytokinesis
targets.description: An actin–myosin cleavage furrow divides the cytoplasm, producing two daughter cells. It overlaps late mitosis.

targets.name: Hematopoietic stem cell
targets.description: A multipotent adult stem cell can self-renew and produce the blood-cell lineages.

targets.name: Self-renewal
targets.description: Stem-cell division can maintain the stem-cell pool as well as provide descendants that differentiate.

targets.name: Myeloid progenitor
targets.description: The myeloid branch gives rise to red blood cells, granulocytes, monocytes, and megakaryocytes that shed platelets. Additional intermediate stages are omitted.

targets.name: Lymphoid progenitor
targets.description: The lymphoid branch gives rise to B cells, T cells, and natural killer cells. The textbook figure shows additional stages and branches.

targets.name: Red blood cell
targets.description: A specialized biconcave cell carries oxygen. Mature human red blood cells have expelled their nucleus.

targets.name: Granulocyte
targets.description: A specialized white blood cell with cytoplasmic granules and a lobed nucleus; the sketch represents a neutrophil.

targets.name: Lymphocyte
targets.description: A specialized white blood cell involved in immune defense; its large nucleus occupies much of the cell.

targets.name: Platelets
targets.description: Small cell fragments shed from megakaryocytes in the myeloid lineage participate in hemostasis. They are not whole nucleated cells.

3.1.stem: Compare simple diffusion, facilitated diffusion, and primary active transport. Use movement direction, proteins, and ATP.
rubric: Simple diffusion moves down a gradient through the lipid bilayer without a transporter or ATP.
Facilitated diffusion moves down a gradient through a carrier or channel without direct ATP use.
Primary active transport directly uses ATP to move material against its gradient, as in the Na/K pump.
3.1.explanation: Simple diffusion moves down a gradient through the lipid bilayer without a transporter or ATP. Facilitated diffusion moves down a gradient through a carrier or channel without direct ATP use. Primary active transport directly uses ATP to move material against its gradient, as in the Na/K pump.

3.4.stem: Explain how a human cell makes a protein from a nuclear gene. Include locations, pre-mRNA processing, and all three RNA roles.
rubric: RNA polymerase transcribes the DNA template to RNA in the nucleus.
A spliceosome removes introns and joins exons in pre-mRNA before mature mRNA exits.
At a cytoplasmic ribosome, mRNA supplies codons, tRNA brings amino acids using anticodons, and rRNA supplies structural/catalytic activity.
3.4.explanation: RNA polymerase transcribes the DNA template to RNA in the nucleus. A spliceosome removes introns and joins exons in pre-mRNA before mature mRNA exits. At a cytoplasmic ribosome, mRNA supplies codons, tRNA brings amino acids using anticodons, and rRNA supplies structural/catalytic activity.

3.5.stem: Explain the chromosome/chromatid count in a normal nucleated human somatic cell before S, after S, and in each daughter after mitosis.
rubric: G1: 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.
After S and before sister separation: 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids because sisters remain joined.
After completed mitosis/cytokinesis: each daughter has 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.
3.5.explanation: G1: 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids. After S and before sister separation: 46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids because sisters remain joined. After completed mitosis/cytokinesis: each daughter has 46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids.

3.6.stem: Compare totipotent, pluripotent, and multipotent stem cells. Give an example of a restricted lineage.
rubric: Totipotent potential includes body and extraembryonic tissues.
Pluripotent potential includes the major body cell types but not complete extraembryonic support for an organism.
Multipotent cells make related lineages, such as hematopoietic stem cells producing blood lineages.
3.6.explanation: Totipotent potential includes body and extraembryonic tissues. Pluripotent potential includes the major body cell types but not complete extraembryonic support for an organism. Multipotent cells make related lineages, such as hematopoietic stem cells producing blood lineages.

4.2.stem: Compare epithelium with connective tissue using arrangement, matrix, vascularity, and function.
rubric: Epithelium forms closely packed sheets with little matrix, apical-basal polarity, and a basement membrane.
Epithelium is avascular and relies on diffusion; its functions include covering, secretion, absorption, and exchange.
Connective tissue generally has more ECM and dispersed cells; its vascularity varies and its functions include support, binding, storage, and transport.

4.3.stem: Compare mesenchymal cells, fibroblasts, and fibrocytes during connective-tissue repair. Include the matrix components.
rubric: Mesenchymal cells are multipotent stem cells able to supply replacement connective-tissue lineages.
Fibroblasts actively build ECM, including ground substance and protein fibers such as collagen.
Fibrocytes are less active cells that maintain existing matrix; they are distinct from mesenchymal stem cells.

Fibroblasts actively build ECM, including ground substance and protein fibers such as collagen. Fibrocytes are less active cells that maintain existing matrix; they are distinct from mesenchymal stem cells.

4.4.stem: Distinguish skeletal, cardiac, and smooth muscle in a microscope image.
rubric: Skeletal: long striated fibers with many peripheral nuclei.
Cardiac: striated branching cells with central nuclei and intercalated discs.
Smooth: spindle-shaped cells, one central nucleus, and no visible striations.
4.4.explanation: Skeletal: long striated fibers with many peripheral nuclei. Cardiac: striated branching cells with central nuclei and intercalated discs. Smooth: spindle-shaped cells, one central nucleus, and no visible striations.

4.6.stem: Compare inflammation, granulation, and scar remodeling in tissue repair.
rubric: Inflammation includes increased blood flow and vascular permeability, immune-cell activity, and debris removal.
Granulation tissue has new vessels and fibroblasts producing collagen.
Remodeling reorganizes collagen; fibrosis leaves scar rather than restoring every original structure.
